name: Phytosphingosine

lead: Phytosphingosine is a fatty-chain amino alcohol that cells use to build ceramides, lipids central to the skin barrier. It appears in some moisturisers and acne-prone skin products.
The sources reviewed contain no human studies of it as a cosmetic.

paras: It is a precursor in sphingolipid and ceramide synthesis; the idea behind skincare use is to supply raw material for barrier lipids.
No cosmetic safety trials were found. The pure chemical carries eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications per Wikipedia.

lead: Phytosphingosine is an 18-carbon sphingoid base (2-aminooctadecane-1,3,4-triol) abundant in plants and fungi and also present in animals. It is a building block of more complex sphingolipids, including certain ceramides.[1][2]

In skincare it is added to products aimed at barrier support and blemish-prone skin, as a ceramide precursor. The sources reviewed contain little cosmetic-specific research on it, so claims about its skin effects rest largely on the general biology of sphingolipids and ceramides.[3]
No human trial of topical phytosphingosine for appearance outcomes was found.

paras: Wikipedia lists the compound's melting point as 102-103 C and flags eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications for the pure chemical.[1] Sphingolipid synthesis, in which sphingoid bases like phytosphingosine are converted to ceramides, has been mapped in detail, including in yeast where phytosphingosine-based ceramides are prominent.[2][4]

Ceramide composition of skin scale has been studied in disease; a 1993 paper described the ceramide composition of psoriatic scale, an example of how skin lipid profiles are linked to barrier health.[3]

Laboratory studies cited by Wikipedia report that phytosphingosine induced programmed cell death in human cancer cells (2003) and showed T-cell-related anti-inflammatory properties in inflammatory bowel disease models (2021).[1] These are not skin-appearance findings.

No studies found on phytosphingosine for skin appearance. A registered trial of skin barrier function and inflammation in ageing exists but its link to phytosphingosine is not established in the sources reviewed.[5]
